situation:
You are a community-college student who works night shifts at a distribution warehouse to stay enrolled. You have an appointment with a benefits counselor (judge) at TIDEWATER BENEFITS CENTER to decide how to spend the little you can set aside for protection.

You share an apartment with a roommate, who has agreed to split rent and utilities; the lease you both signed runs another nine months. Your hours are real but not guaranteed; the warehouse cut the night crew last winter. If your hours were cut, your roommate would be left covering the whole apartment. The used car you drive to work and class has 140,000 miles.

Your employer's disability coverage can only be added during the enrollment window that closes this month. Signing up costs $19 a month, money you now put toward the car repair fund, and leaves nothing set aside if the transmission fails. Buying the three-year extended warranty instead costs $900 up front and leaves your wages unprotected if an injury keeps you off the night shift.

The benefits counselor (judge) wants you to weigh how much of your income each choice actually protects, explain what you would lose by going without health coverage, and recommend which one to buy. The counselor (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
